issues.legal_issue: An agent who agrees to insure the principal’s goods and fails to do so is liable for the uncompensated loss when an intervening compensation scheme pays less for uninsured goods, if that shortfall directly results from the failure to insure.
material_facts: The agents were instructed and agreed to insure goods held pending shipment, but did not insure them.
The goods were destroyed in a harbour explosion and ensuing fire.
A later compensation scheme provided greater compensation for insured goods than for uninsured goods, regardless of the terms of the insurance policy.
The principals sought the remaining loss from the agents after credit for the compensation received.
issues.conclusion: The unpaid balance was a direct consequence of the agents’ failure to insure, not remote damage. The later compensation scheme did not break the chain of causation or create a new liability; it supplied the measure for assessing the loss. The contention that an ordinary fire policy excluded explosion damage did not defeat the claim, since compensation under the scheme depended on the existence of a policy rather than its terms.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 211 and 212 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agent must make good loss directly resulting from neglect or misconduct, but not loss indirectly or remotely caused. The applicable damages principles include the direct-consequence approach discussed in In re Polemis and Weld-Blundell v. Stephens; the contract-damages rules in Hadley v. Baxendale and Monarch Steamship Co. Ltd. v. Karlshamns Oljefabriker; the restitutio in integrum principle in Livingstone v. Rawyards Coal Co.; and the causation and damages discussions in British Westinghouse Electric & Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v. Underground Electric Railways Co. of London, Liesbosch (Owners) v. Edison (Owners), Smith, Hogg & Co. Ltd. v. Black Sea & Baltic General Insurance Co. Ltd., and Standard Oil Co. of New York v. Clan Line Steamers Ltd. The Court also relied on the principles concerning an agent who undertakes insurance in Smith v. Lascelles and Tickel v. Short. The majority treated the compensation scheme as quantifying the loss rather than creating the agent’s liability. Patanjali Sastri J. dissented, considering the shortfall to result from independent events and therefore to be remote.

rule.if: agent_principal_damages_claim and agent_agreed_to_insure and agent_failed_to_insure and goods_destroyed_in_explosion_or_fire and compensation_scheme_paid_less_for_uninsured_goods

predicates.agent_principal_damages_claim: A principal seeks damages from an agent for loss connected with the agent’s handling of the principal’s goods.
predicates.agent_agreed_to_insure: The agent agreed to insure the principal’s goods.
predicates.agent_failed_to_insure: The agent did not obtain the agreed insurance.
predicates.goods_destroyed_in_explosion_or_fire: The goods were destroyed by an explosion or resulting fire.
predicates.compensation_scheme_paid_less_for_uninsu: A compensation scheme provided less compensation for uninsured goods than for insured goods.

issues.definition: When a principal claims damages from an agent who agreed but failed to insure goods destroyed by an explosion or fire, and a compensation scheme pays less for uninsured goods, the rule makes the agent liable for the direct uncompensated loss.

issues.legal_issue: A claim against an agent for failing to perform an agency duty is not barred merely because the loss used to measure damages arose from an explosion.
material_facts: The agents sought payment for goods purchased on the principals’ account, and the principals counterclaimed or sought a set-off based on the agents’ failure to insure those goods as agreed.
The claimed liability was based on the agents’ alleged misconduct in the agency, including the duty or agreement to insure, its non-performance, and resulting loss.
The explosion compensation scheme barred other claims for compensation or damages for property loss due to or arising out of the explosion.
issues.conclusion: The counterclaim was not barred. Its cause of action was the agents’ misconduct in the agency, and the amount of damages was not part of the cause of action. Patanjali Sastri J. dissented, reasoning that the claimed loss arose out of the explosion and was therefore within the bar.
issues.legal_principle: The majority construed section 18(2) of the Bombay Explosion (Compensation) Ordinance, 1944, as not barring a claim whose cause of action is an agent’s breach of duty in the agency, even though explosion-related loss determines the damages. The cause of action is complete upon alleging a duty or agreement, failure to perform it, and resulting loss; the quantum of damages is for the court to determine. The dissent considered the bar to turn on whether the loss was due to or arose out of the explosion, rather than on the legal basis of the claim.

rule.if: agency_misconduct_claim_against_agent and agent_duty_to_insure_goods and agent_failed_to_perform_duty and explosion_related_loss_used_to_measure_damages

predicates.agency_misconduct_claim_against_agent: A principal asserts a claim against an agent based on misconduct in the agency relationship.
predicates.agent_duty_to_insure_goods: The agent had a duty or agreement to insure the principal’s goods.
predicates.agent_failed_to_perform_duty: The agent failed to perform that duty or agreement.
predicates.explosion_related_loss_used_to_measure_d: Loss associated with an explosion is used to calculate the damages claimed against the agent.

issues.definition: When a principal’s claim against an agent is based on agency misconduct and failure to insure, the use of explosion-related loss to measure damages does not make the claim barred by the compensation scheme.
